newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FISHERFOLK CRITICISE S.AFRICAN MARINE POLICY.
newsitem.headline: FISHERFOLK CRITICISE S.AFRICAN MARINE POLICY.

text.p: Small-scale fishermen criticised South Africa's draft marine resources policy on Thursday, saying access to fish should depend on old-fashioned skill rather than money power.

Andy Johnson, chairman of the Informal Fisherworkers Association (IFA), told a news conference the fisheries white paper published by Environment Minister Pallo Jordan last month was biased in favour of big companies like Irvin & Johnson and Sea Harvest .
"We are being ignored and treated as outsiders because we do not have the money and the power that spells influence in politics," said Johnson, who put IFA membership at 2,800.
"We say access to the sea must be equitably distributed to the have-nots as well as the haves."
He said he agreed with the government policy of imposing a total allowable catch (TAC) for each species, but said the idea of individual quotas for companies or individuals should be scrapped.
Fishermen should be allowed to catch as much as they could until the TAC was reached, and the amount each person caught would depend on his skill, Johnson said.
"We see this as a system where creativity and hard work are rewarded and the monopolising interests of big business contained and controlled."

An advisor to the IFA, Nalini Nayak of the Indian-based International Collective for the Support of Fish Workers, told the news conference the white paper appeared to have been drafted without adequate recognition of developments in other parts of the world.
She said it would perpetuate the system which had led to the collapse of fish stocks in the northern hemisphere by promoting industrial fishing as opposed to artisan-style fishing.
Artisan fishing including hook and line fishing as well as trawling, but was carried out in a more targetted way that did not deplete fish stocks, Nayak said.
She said South Africa should encourage labour intensive processing of fish such as drying, salting or fermenting which used free energy from the sun.
The rest of Africa provided a big market for dried fish, she said, adding that South Africa was too oriented towards selling to Japan, the United States and Europe.
Johnson said his organisation would seek to have fisheries policy changed through discussion with Jordan and members of parliament.
In presenting the white paper, Jordan said the aim was not to break up the major fishing companies but to encourage them to empower the kind of fishermen represented by the IFA.
He said he wanted to redress the skewed legacy of apartheid but the big companies provided jobs and had the resources to compete internationally.
